title: Artificial Intelligence Cannot Plan
author: Ben Newmark
summary: Ben Newmark argues that AI's promise to save teachers time on lesson planning rests on a category error: it confuses planning with resourcing. Resources, slides, worksheets, booklets, are products of planning, he argues, but the actual thinking about how a specific idea should be taught to a specific, real class in front of you is a human process AI cannot replicate. He traces this confusion back before AI, to the era of shared drives and TES resource-sharing, arguing that borrowed resources have always been less effective than self-made ones because they lack the framing decisions (how to introduce a slide, what an image is meant to signify) that only the planner's own thinking encodes. Newmark predicts that if AI-generated resourcing further collapses the time planning appears to take, teachers won't actually gain free time, they'll simply be assigned something else to fill it, drawing an analogy to how email replaced pigeon-holes and data-drop cycles replaced older marking regimes without ever producing the promised time savings. He closes on a note of foreboding, questioning what teachers will be expected to do instead once AI 'normalises' planning as a fast, low-effort task.
points: Newmark's central claim is a category distinction: AI is very good at producing resources (slides, worksheets) but planning is the underlying human thinking about how to teach specific content to a specific class, which AI cannot do.

He traces the resourcing-versus-planning confusion back to pre-AI shared-drive and TES culture, arguing borrowed resources have always underperformed self-made ones because they lack the planner's framing decisions.

He predicts AI won't actually free up teacher time, drawing a historical analogy: past labor-saving innovations (email replacing pigeon-holes, changed marking regimes) never produced lasting time savings, just different demands.

He frames the risk not as AI failing outright but as AI succeeding at producing plausible-looking outputs quickly, which then get mistaken for genuine planning and erode the thinking process planning is supposed to represent.
quotes: AI can plan your lessons, saving you time and easing your workload. Except it won't, because it can't, because planning is a human process that only happens in human minds.
Those that think AI can plan make an important category error because they don’t understand what planning really is and have confused it with creating resources, which AI is very good at.
Planning is a teacher thinking about the material and how best this can be taught to a particular real life flesh-and-blood class. AI cannot do this.
Tasks and activities that made intuitive sense to the person making the resource made far less sense to a different person because they lack nuance on how each slide should be introduced and framed.
AI is so problematic because it allows the products of planning, resources and timed sequencing, to be produced with minimal thought.
Everything I have ever known in twenty-years working in education convinces me when something is taken away from us it is always replaced by something else.
